analysis.one_liner: Nearly triples and makes permanent the tax deduction for business owners' pass-through income.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have enlarged the pass-through tax deduction from 20% to 43% of business income, drew zero cosponsors and died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have greatly expanded the "pass-through" deduction created by the 2017 tax law, which lets business owners deduct part of their business income instead of paying normal income tax on it. It would have raised the deduction from 20% to 43% of business income (a top rate of about 21%), made it permanent, removed the limit tied to wages a business pays, and allowed even high-earning professionals like lawyers, consultants, and hedge fund managers to claim it. People who work as employees would get nothing, no matter how much they earn.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of pass-through businesses — partnerships, S corporations, and sole proprietorships — whose business income would be taxed at a much lower effective rate. The gains would be largest for high earners in fields the current law excludes when income is high: law firms, consultancies, financial firms, and private medical practices. Genuinely small business owners would also get a real tax cut, but the biggest dollar benefits would flow to the highest-income owners, because the deduction is worth the most to people in the top brackets. Employees get no benefit at all.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the qualified business income deduction from 20% to 43% of business income, which caps the top effective tax rate on that income at about 21%, far below the 37% top individual rate.
Makes the deduction permanent by deleting the section that schedules it to expire, so the benefit never sunsets.
Repeals the limit that ties the deduction to wages a business actually pays, letting owners claim the full break regardless of payroll.
Removes the exclusion for high-earning service businesses, so lawyers, consultants, financial firms, and doctors could claim the deduction at any income level.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, since the bill contains no offsetting revenue and would enlarge a permanent tax break, adding to deficits. That cost falls on everyone else — including the employees who do similar work as business owners but receive no deduction.

drawbacks.text: The deduction goes only to business owners. Two people doing identical work — one a partner, one on salary — would be taxed completely differently, and the employee gets nothing.
Repealing the wage-based limit removes the guardrail designed to stop owners from recharacterizing their own salary as business income to pay less tax.
The bill has no way to pay for itself; enlarging and making the deduction permanent would add substantial revenue loss to the deficit on top of the existing 2017 tax law.
The largest dollar benefits go to the highest earners, since the deduction scales with income and the bill removes the income-based exclusion for service professionals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Small business owners would genuinely pay less tax, and a simpler, uniform deduction has some appeal. But the design is heavily skewed: by repealing both the wage limit and the exclusion for high-earning service fields, it directs the biggest benefits to wealthy professionals rather than small shops, and it hands the break to owners while excluding their employees. With no offset and no sunset, the long-run cost to the Treasury would be large relative to any broad public benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Ways and Means Committee, which never held a hearing or voted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the bill on May 23, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor at any point.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote ever followed the referral; the bill sat in committee until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers overall are better off that it died: no enlarged permanent tax cut was added to the deficit, and the existing 20% deduction kept its limits and expiration date. High-earning business owners, who stood to gain the most, came out no better than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers who would have funded the cut

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it was his alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: Richard Neal

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup during the two years it sat in his committee.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after receiving the referral; the record shows nothing beyond it.

sides.party_line_note: A lone Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors and no vote ever held, so no party split is on record.

industries.industry: High-income professional firms (law, consulting, finance, private medicine)
industries.note: Current law denies these owners the deduction once income is high; the bill removes that exclusion, letting the highest-earning professionals pay about a 21% top rate on business income. Their gain comes at the Treasury's expense, while salaried employees in the same fields get nothing.

They would receive a real, permanent tax cut, worth more because the wage-based limit would be repealed. But the benefit is funded by deficits and is worth far more in dollars to the wealthy than to a typical small shop.
